summary: Extends Proxy Mobile IPv6 with IPv4 support. It lets a mobile node keep an IPv4 home address while moving, and allows the network elements to exchange signaling over an IPv4 transport. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5844 extends Proxy Mobile IPv6 so a mobile node can keep an IPv4 home address while it moves within a domain. It also lets the network's mobility gateways exchange signaling over IPv4, and the two features can be enabled separately.

subtitle: Adds IPv4 address mobility and IPv4 transport options to Proxy Mobile IPv6.

tldr.problem: Base Proxy Mobile IPv6 supports IPv6 home address mobility and requires IPv6 transport between its mobility entities.
tldr.mechanism: New signaling options let a mobile access gateway request an IPv4 home address from a local mobility anchor. Separate extensions carry signaling and data tunnels over IPv4.
tldr.outcome: The mobile node can keep its IPv4 home address as it changes access points. Address mobility and IPv4 transport can be used independently.

today: RFC 5844 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2010. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Two Independent IPv4 Features
sections.content:
Proxy Mobile IPv6 originally provides IPv6 home address mobility and requires IPv6 transport between the mobile access gateway (MAG) and local mobility anchor (LMA). RFC 5844 adds IPv4 home address mobility and IPv4 transport support.

The features are independent. A mobile node can use IPv4, IPv6, or both, while the MAG and LMA can exchange signaling over an IPv4 network. The specification assumes dual-stack mobility entities and does not support a MAG behind NAT when connecting to the LMA.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC adds two separate capabilities: a mobile node can keep an IPv4 address as it moves, and the network can carry mobility signaling over IPv4. A deployment can use either capability or both.

sections.title: Addresses and Mobility Roles
sections.content:
The mobile node's IPv4 home address is anchored at its LMA. The MAG's IPv4 egress address is the IPv4 Proxy Care-of Address, and the LMA's IPv4 egress address is the IPv4-LMAA used for IPv4 transport.

IPv4 and IPv6 addresses for one mobile-node interface belong to one mobility session and one Binding Cache entry. A mobile node using multiple interfaces receives a unique IPv4 address for each interface.
sections.plainLanguage: The LMA keeps track of the mobile node's home address, while the MAG serves the network where the node is currently attached. The RFC keeps IPv4 and IPv6 state for one interface in the same mobility session.

sections.title: Requesting and Keeping an IPv4 Home Address
sections.content:
When IPv4 mobility is needed, the MAG sends a Proxy Binding Update with exactly one IPv4 Home Address Request option. An all-zero requested address asks the LMA to allocate one; a non-zero value requests that specific address. IPv6 home-prefix options are included only when IPv6 mobility is also requested.

The LMA checks authorization and resources, creates or updates the mobility binding, establishes a bidirectional tunnel, and returns the IPv4 Home Address Reply and default-router information. After a handoff, the new MAG registers the node and the LMA updates forwarding to the new attachment.
sections.plainLanguage: The MAG asks the LMA for an IPv4 home address, either requesting allocation or naming a specific address. After a move, the new MAG registers the node so traffic for that same address reaches its new connection.

sections.title: Mobility Options and Status Codes
sections.content:
RFC 5844 defines four mobility options: IPv4 Home Address Request (type 36), IPv4 Home Address Reply (type 37), IPv4 Default-Router Address (type 38), and IPv4 DHCP Support Mode (type 39). The DHCP mode flag tells the MAG to act as a relay when it is 0 and a server when it is 1.

The reply option reports success or failure, and the new Proxy Binding Acknowledgement status codes 170 through 173 report authorization and assignment problems.
sections.plainLanguage: New message options carry the requested address, the assigned address, the default router, and the DHCP mode. Status codes explain why an address request was rejected.

sections.title: Delivering the Address with DHCP
sections.content:
The RFC describes a DHCP server or DHCP relay on the MAG. With a local server, the MAG offers the address assigned by the LMA and supplies the subnet mask and router information. A stable DHCP server identifier lets a renewal reach the MAG after a handoff.

With a relay, the MAG adds relay-agent information that carries the assigned address as a hint. The MAG drops an offer for a different address, and DHCP messages crossing administrative boundaries need protection.
sections.plainLanguage: The MAG can tell the mobile node its assigned address using DHCP. Whether the MAG runs a DHCP server or relays messages to another server, it checks that DHCP uses the address assigned by the LMA.

sections.title: Carrying Signaling and Data over IPv4
sections.content:
Using an IPv6-over-IPv4 tunnel for base Proxy Mobile IPv6 adds 40 octets to each tunneled packet. RFC 5844 instead carries the Mobility Header in UDP over IPv4; signaling uses destination port 5436 and the Mobility Header checksum is zero while UDP supplies the checksum.

Data can use IPv4, IPv4-UDP on port 5437, IPv4-UDP-TLV, or IPv4-GRE encapsulation. The MAG and LMA negotiate whether UDP encapsulation is used. The RFC describes optional IPsec ESP protection for signaling and payload traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: The MAG and LMA can exchange signaling directly over IPv4 instead of wrapping IPv6 in IPv4. They can also tunnel mobile-node data using one of the specified IPv4 encapsulations.
